title: Newton method and curvature correction
description: Solve a full Newton correction, compare gradient descent from the same point, and work a fresh practice with saddle/singular counterexamples.
source_short: Lecture4 PDF p.33-36,47-52 / full Newton eta=1 / N4.3
source: Lecture4 PDF pages33-36: scalar curvature; pages47-52: normalized multivariate update and Hessian issues, eta included on page50. numerical-practice.md N4.3.

pages.title: Newton uses slope and curvature together
pages.subtitle: Start with one parameter, where the Hessian is just a second derivative.
blocks: The full Newton correction divides slope by curvature. In this exact positive-curvature quadratic, it lands at the minimum in one step.
Gradient descent uses a chosen rate times the slope. Newton adjusts the correction using curvature.

pages.title: Map the lecture formula to a linear system
pages.subtitle: Evaluate the gradient and Hessian at the same original parameter vector.
blocks: Lecture4 PDF page50 includes a rate eta. Here eta_N=1 means a full Newton step. We use g as a column gradient; tuples below list its components.
The correction s equals H-inverse times g. The actual displacement is -s. Some notes instead name the signed displacement Delta and solve H Delta = -g.
Both conventions give the same update. Solving the system avoids explicitly forming the inverse.

pages.title: Compute the mixed-quadratic ingredients
pages.subtitle: Reuse the Lesson21 function and the same start for both methods.
blocks: Thus H has rows (3,1) and (1,3). Its positive eigenvalues 2 and 4 were derived in Lesson21.

pages.title: Solve for the Newton correction by elimination
pages.subtitle: The matrix equation Hs=g becomes two ordinary equations.
blocks: Check the solution: 3(2)+0=6 and 2+3(0)=2. The correction is (2,0), while the displacement is (-2,0).

pages.title: Optional check: the two-by-two inverse
pages.subtitle: The linear solve is sufficient; this shows why the inverse formula agrees.
blocks: For rows (a,b) and (c,d), the inverse has rows (d,-b) and (-c,a), all divided by ad-bc. This requires a nonzero determinant.
Therefore H inverse has rows (3,-1)/8 and (-1,3)/8.
These are exactly the correction components found by elimination. Do not invert each matrix entry separately.

pages.title: Compare gradient descent from the same start
pages.subtitle: Use eta_G=0.1; this is an alternative update, not an extra Newton step.
blocks: Both lower this quadratic. Their directions differ because Newton accounts for the mixed curvature rather than multiplying every gradient coordinate by the same scalar.

pages.title: Two alternative arrows from one starting point
pages.subtitle: Contours connect points with equal loss.
blocks: The arrows share the original point (2,0). The gradient-descent point is not an intermediate stage of the Newton calculation.

pages.title: Why the exact quadratic finishes in one full step
pages.subtitle: The local quadratic model is the entire function in this special case.
blocks: For an exact positive-definite quadratic and an exact solve, a full Newton step reaches the unique minimum from any starting point. General neural-network losses do not have this guarantee.
A damped Newton step keeps the lecture rate below one here. It moves only partway along the correction, so the one-step result no longer applies.
The Hessian can also be expensive, singular or indefinite. These issues are separate from the arithmetic of a successful small quadratic example.

pages.title: An invertible Hessian can lead to a saddle
pages.subtitle: Newton seeks a stationary point; that point need not be a minimum.
blocks: H is diagonal (1,-1), which is invertible but indefinite. Solve Hs=g: sx=0 and -sy=-1, so s=(0,1).
The loss increases and the origin is a saddle. Reaching the exact stationary point in one step is not the same as reaching a minimum.

pages.title: A singular Hessian makes the raw formula undefined
pages.subtitle: Even a true minimum may have zero curvature at that point.
blocks: The origin is a minimum because w-to-the-fourth is nonnegative. But the raw Newton division cannot be evaluated there. Do not call 0/0 a zero correction.
A practical method needs an appropriate stopping test or a modified step when the curvature system cannot be solved.

blocks: Common errors: using H inverse entry-by-entry, evaluating H and g at different points, adding s when it was defined by Hs=g, dropping the lecture rate without declaring a full step, or assuming invertible means positive definite.
